notes: Ruling slot 4 = MSZMP (icon HUN_emerging_communism: MD's Munkáspárt is the MSZMP's direct, same-named successor). Independent Smallholders moved from MD slot 20 to slot 1 (starting popularity; in 1945-47 the FKGP was the Western-oriented centre-right mass party), keeping its MD sprite. NEM reformers (Nyers, Fock) as 'Az új mechanizmus' in slot 13, anti-reform hardliners (Biszku, Komócsin, Gáspár) in slot 6, state security BM III in slot 7, Imre Nagy group in 19, Budapest School in 5. Islamic slots use Arab student circles in Budapest and the Muslim convert Gyula Germanus.

0.name: Magyar Harcosok Bajtársi Közössége
0.text:
The Association of Hungarian Veterans was founded in 1947 by General András Zákó among officers of the Royal Hungarian Army who had retreated west with their units in 1945. From its centre in Munich it runs chapters across Western Europe, the Americas and Australia, and in the early Cold War it supplied couriers and informants to American and West German intelligence.

Its members honour the memory of Regent Miklós Horthy and want a Hungary restored to order by a disciplined, anti-communist officer corps under Western protection, built on Christian and national values and an army free of political commissars. Its leverage lies in its old intelligence contacts, its veterans' newspapers and its claim to speak for the military tradition of pre-1945 Hungary.

1.name: Független Kisgazda-, Földmunkás- és Polgári Párt
1.native_full: Független Kisgazda-, Földmunkás- és Polgári Párt
1.text:
The Independent Smallholders' Party won 57 per cent of the vote in the free elections of November 1945, only to be broken up by Mátyás Rákosi's 'salami tactics': its Secretary-General Béla Kovács was arrested by the Soviets in 1947 and Prime Minister Ferenc Nagy was forced into exile. Revived in 1956, it has no legal existence in 1970. Ferenc Nagy lives in the United States, while Monsignor Béla Varga chairs the émigré Hungarian Committee in New York.

The party stands for private peasant property, parliamentary democracy, Christian values and close friendship with the West. Collectivisation has destroyed its old base of smallholders, yet among older villagers and the provincial middle class its name still recalls the last freely elected government. Its leverage lies in memory and legitimacy rather than organisation.
1.wiki: Independent Smallholders, Agrarian Workers and Civic Party

2.name: Irodalmi Újság
2.text:
The Literary Gazette was the weekly of the Hungarian Writers' Union that helped spark the revolution of 1956. Refounded by émigré writers in London in 1957 and published in Paris since 1962 under the editorship of Tibor Méray, it is the leading forum of the democratic emigration, uniting former reform communists, liberals and populists such as Pál Ignotus and Tamás Aczél.

Its circle stands for a free press, a multiparty parliament, the rule of law and a Hungary integrated into a democratic Europe, faithful to the legacy of 1956. It rejects both Kádár's dictatorship and the nostalgia of the Horthyist right. Its leverage is moral and intellectual: smuggled copies, Radio Free Europe broadcasts that quote it, and a network of writers who are read at home in secret.

3.name: Magyarországi Szociáldemokrata Párt
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party of Hungary, founded in 1890, was forced into a merger with the Communists in 1948 while its independent leaders went to prison. Revived during the revolution of 1956, it sent its chairwoman Anna Kéthly into Imre Nagy's last cabinet. Since then Kéthly has led the party in exile from Belgium, where it is represented in the Socialist International.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, free trade unions, workers' participation and a mixed economy, in the tradition of Central European social democracy and in friendship with the Western labour movement. At home its old cadres survive as pensioners and skilled workers in Budapest's factory districts. Its leverage lies in its international recognition, its links to Western labour parties and the respect that Kéthly's name still commands.

4.name: Magyar Szocialista Munkáspárt
4.text:
The Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party was formed by János Kádár on 1 November 1956 from the ruins of Rákosi's party and has ruled with Soviet backing ever since. Kádár, First Secretary ever since, has moved from the reprisals that ended with Imre Nagy's execution to a policy of reconciliation summed up in his phrase 'whoever is not against us is with us'. Jenő Fock heads the government and Pál Losonczi the Presidential Council.

Since 1 January 1968 the party has staked its future on the New Economic Mechanism, giving enterprises freedom over prices and profits within the plan. 'Goulash communism' trades quiet for rising living standards, while loyalty to Moscow, proven in Czechoslovakia in 1968, buys room for reform. It commands the nomenklatura, the security organs and the Soviet garrison.

5.name: Budapesti iskola
5.text:
The Budapest School is the circle of philosophers and sociologists formed around György Lukács, who at 84 still writes in his flat on the Belgrade embankment. Its core members are Ágnes Heller, Ferenc Fehér, György Márkus and Mihály Vajda, joined by András Hegedüs, prime minister in 1955-1956 and now a critical sociologist. In August 1968 several of them signed the Korčula declaration condemning the invasion of Czechoslovakia, and they are under growing pressure from the party's ideologists.

They seek a democratic, self-managed socialism built on workers' councils, the satisfaction of 'radical needs' and the critique of bureaucracy, close in spirit to the Yugoslav Praxis group and the Western New Left. They have no mass following, but their books travel abroad and shape the young left.

6.name: A Biszku-szárny
6.text:
The Biszku Wing is the hardline current in the Political Committee that has never trusted the New Economic Mechanism. Its figurehead is Béla Biszku, Interior Minister during the reprisals after 1956 and now Central Committee secretary for the armed and security organs, flanked by the party secretaries Zoltán Komócsin and Árpád Pullai and by the trade union chief Sándor Gáspár.

They complain that the reform enriches managers, private plot farmers and 'speculators' while industrial workers fall behind, and they warn that market mechanisms opened the road to the Prague Spring. They want stricter planning, ideological vigilance and close alignment with Brezhnev's Moscow. Their leverage lies in the Workers' Militia, the unions, the heavy-industry lobby and the Soviet comrades who share their doubts about Hungary's experiment.

7.name: Belügyminisztérium III. Főcsoportfőnökség
7.english: Main Directorate III of the Ministry of the Interior
7.text:
Main Directorate III of the Ministry of the Interior is Hungary's state security service, created in 1962 when the political police inherited from the 1950s was reorganised under tighter party control. Under Interior Minister András Benkei its departments handle counter-intelligence, the struggle against 'internal reaction', military counter-intelligence and surveillance of the churches, the intelligentsia and the emigration.

As a power bloc it values order above ideology: a dense web of informers, a silent dissident scene, controlled contacts with the West and no repeat of 1956. Kádár has curbed its excesses, preferring surveillance and career pressure to show trials, yet its files cover the whole of society. Its leverage lies in information, in the power of arrest and in its close working ties with the Soviet KGB.

8.name: Usrat Jabal Amil
8.text:
Among the Lebanese students sent to Budapest's universities on scholarships arranged by the Lebanese Communist Party are many sons of Shia villages in Jabal Amil and the Beqaa. A small circle of them has turned from Marxism toward Imam Musa al-Sadr, the Iranian-born cleric of Tyre who in 1969 became head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council and speaks for the 'deprived' of southern Lebanon.

They want social justice, schools, roads and dignity for the Shia poor within a reformed Lebanese state, joining religious revival to a modern, almost social-democratic vocabulary. They distrust both the Maronite establishment and the Palestinian guerrillas whose raids draw Israeli fire onto the south. In Hungary their leverage is nil, but as future engineers and doctors they will carry Sadr's movement home.

9.name: Ansar al-Marja'iyya
9.text:
The Partisans of the Marja'iyya are a handful of Iraqi Shia students at the Budapest Technical University and the medical school, sons of merchant and clerical families from Najaf, Karbala and Kadhimiya. Their loyalty belongs to Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim, the supreme marja of the Shia world, whose clash with the Ba'athist regime in 1969 drove his followers underground, and they listen closely to the exiled Iranian Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, now teaching in Najaf.

They regard Ba'athism and communism as godless tyranny and hold that legitimate authority belongs to the learned jurists of Islam. They keep the Muharram mourning in private rooms and send religious dues to Najaf. Their leverage is minimal, but their ties to the seminaries make them messengers of a militant clerical movement.

10.name: Germanus Gyula köre
10.text:
The Germanus Circle gathers Hungary's few Muslims around Gyula Germanus, the 85-year-old orientalist who embraced Islam in India in the early 1930s, made the pilgrimage to Mecca and described it in his book Allah Akbar!. A member of the Arabic academies of Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad, he is courted by Arab diplomats and keeps alive the memory of the Islamic community recognised by Hungarian law in 1916.

The circle seeks no political power. It hopes for a registered Muslim congregation, a prayer room and care for monuments such as the tomb of the dervish Gül Baba on Rose Hill, and it looks to the religious establishment of Cairo and Mecca for support. Its leverage lies in prestige and Hungary's wish for good relations with the Arab world.

11.name: Shabab al-Tahrir
11.text:
The Liberation Youth is a cell of Jordanian and Syrian students in Budapest who brought with them the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. Banned across the Arab world, the party survives in tight study circles; in Budapest its few adherents meet in hostel rooms and pray together in a private flat on Fridays.

They hold that every existing state, from King Hussein's Jordan to the Ba'athist and communist regimes, is illegitimate, and that only a restored caliphate ruling by the sharia can unite the Muslims and recover Palestine. They reject elections, preferring to win over officers and elites for a single decisive seizure of power. Watched by Hungarian state security, they have no influence beyond their own conviction.

12.name: Usrat al-Mithaq
12.text:
The Charter Circle unites Sudanese students in Budapest who belonged at home to the Islamic Charter Front, the political arm of the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood led by the Sorbonne-trained lawyer Hasan al-Turabi. Since Colonel Ja'far Nimeiry's leftist coup of May 1969 banned the parties and jailed Turabi, these students live in a curious exile: educated by a communist state while their movement is persecuted by a government friendly to the communists.

They follow the Brotherhood's gradual path of personal piety, study circles, charity and an Islamic constitution won by persuasion and elections rather than conspiracy. Anti-communist but courteous toward their hosts. Their leverage in Hungary is negligible, yet they keep in touch with Brotherhood students across Europe and will return home as cadres of the Islamic movement.

13.name: Az új mechanizmus
13.text:
The New Mechanism is the reform bloc that designed and now administers the economic reform launched on 1 January 1968. Its architect is Rezső Nyers, Central Committee secretary for the economy and a former Social Democrat; around him stand Prime Minister Jenő Fock, Deputy Prime Minister Lajos Fehér, protector of the cooperatives and household plots, and Béla Csikós-Nagy of the National Materials and Price Office, backed by the economists of the Academy.

They believe that prices, profits and enterprise initiative must replace compulsory plan targets, that trade and credit from the West are indispensable, and that prosperity secures socialism better than repression. Their leverage lies in results, full shops and rising wages, and in Kádár's protection, which may not survive Soviet suspicion.

14.name: Magyar Katolikus Egyház
14.text:
The Catholic Church is Hungary's largest denomination, with some six million baptised faithful. Its primate, Cardinal József Mindszenty, has lived as a refugee in the United States Embassy in Budapest since November 1956, while the bishops govern under the 1964 partial agreement between the Holy See and Budapest, which lets bishops be appointed with state consent. The State Office for Church Affairs and the regime-sponsored 'peace priests' watch every parish.

Under Archbishop József Ijjas of Kalocsa and his fellow bishops the hierarchy follows the Vatican's cautious Ostpolitik, seeking to save parishes, seminaries and the few permitted Catholic schools rather than confront the state. Underground base communities such as Father György Bulányi's Bokor keep a more defiant faith. Its leverage is the loyalty of the countryside and its moral authority.

15.name: A nagyvállalati lobbi
15.text:
The Big Enterprise Lobby is the informal alliance of the directors of Hungary's great state works and trusts: the Csepel Works, Ikarus, Tungsram, Ganz-MÁVAG, the Danube Iron Works and the Rába works of Győr, whose general director Ede Horváth has become a national figure. Granted new autonomy by the reform of 1968, these managers command tens of thousands of workers, export earnings and close ties to ministers and county party chiefs.

They want investment funds, cheap credit, protection from small competitors and the freedom to strike their own deals with Western firms, all within the safety of state ownership. They welcome autonomy but resent market discipline. Their leverage lies in their sheer size, their influence over the unions and the fact that the economy cannot run without them.

16.name: A Liska-kör
16.text:
The Liska Circle gathers young economists and engineers around Tibor Liska, the maverick economist whose essay Ökonosztát of the early 1960s proposed a radical model of 'entrepreneurial socialism'. Too radical even for the architects of the 1968 reform, Liska argues his case in seminars and journals, sustained by an enthusiastic student following.

His model would lease every piece of social property to the highest bidder, let individuals run firms at their own risk through personal accounts, free all prices and open the economy to world markets, while guaranteeing every citizen a social inheritance. It is the closest thing to free-market thinking tolerated in the Soviet bloc. Its leverage is intellectual: the circle is shaping a generation of economists who see the plan as an obstacle rather than a tool.

17.name: Herman Ottó örökösei
17.text:
The Heirs of Ottó Herman are the naturalists, foresters and ornithologists who follow the founder of Hungarian ornithology. They work in the Natural History Museum, the universities and the county nature conservation services, and their best-known public voice is István Homoki Nagy, whose nature films and books have made the wildlife of the Hungarian forests and marshes popular with millions.

They campaign for national parks on the Hortobágy puszta and in the Bükk hills, for the protection of bustards, herons and birds of prey, and they warn that sewage, algae and holiday building are spoiling Lake Balaton while plans for great dams threaten the Danube. Their leverage lies in scientific authority and a growing public love of the countryside.

18.name: Nemzeti Parasztpárt
18.text:
The National Peasant Party was founded in 1939 by populist writers who had exposed the misery of the landless rural poor, and in 1945 it championed the land reform that broke up the great estates. Absorbed into the communist-led front after 1949 and briefly revived as the Petőfi Party in 1956, it survives in 1970 as a network of veterans rather than an organisation. Its old chairman Péter Veres, the peasant novelist, and the sociologist Ferenc Erdei remain respected public figures.

Its tradition is a 'third road' between capitalism and Soviet collectivism: cooperative villages run by those who farm them, rural schooling and culture, and a socialism rooted in national life rather than imported from Moscow. Its leverage lies in its prestige among cooperative farmers and provincial intellectuals.

19.name: A Nagy Imre-csoport
19.text:
The Imre Nagy Group is the name the regime gave to the reform communists who stood with Imre Nagy in 1953 and 1956 and were tried with him in 1958, when Nagy was hanged. The survivors were freed by the amnesties of 1960 to 1963 and now live under surveillance in modest jobs: the agrarian economist Ferenc Donáth, the journalist Miklós Vásárhelyi and Sándor Kopácsi, the Budapest police chief of 1956.

They believe in a Hungarian road to socialism: democracy within the party, workers' councils, respect for the peasantry, national independence and the neutrality Nagy proclaimed on 1 November 1956. They reject both Stalinism and capitalist restoration. Their leverage lies in the unspoken legitimacy of 1956, which the regime cannot mention and the nation cannot forget.

20.name: A népi-nemzeti írók
20.text:
The National Populist Writers continue the populist movement of the 1930s, which championed the peasantry against both the gentry and the cosmopolitan city. Their elders are the poet Gyula Illyés and the novelist and essayist László Németh, honoured by the regime yet independent in spirit; a younger generation includes the poet Sándor Csoóri and the playwright István Csurka.

They put the nation first: the fate of three million Hungarians in Romania, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union, the collapsing birth rate, the dying village and the threat of a consumerist, rootless Budapest. They distrust urban liberal and Marxist intellectuals alike and see both the Soviet empire and Western capitalism as dangers to Hungarian identity. Their leverage lies in literary prestige, the Writers' Union and a large provincial readership.

21.name: Hungarista Mozgalom
21.text:
The Hungarist Movement is the émigré continuation of Ferenc Szálasi's Arrow Cross Party, which ruled Hungary during the terror of 1944-1945 and murdered thousands of Jews in Budapest. Szálasi was executed in 1946; his surviving followers regrouped in Austria, West Germany, Argentina, Australia and the United States, where veterans such as Árpád Henney keep the movement alive through newsletters, congresses and commemorations.

It preaches Szálasi's 'Hungarism': an authoritarian corporate state, a Greater Hungary dominating the Carpathian Basin, militant anti-communism and open antisemitism. Inside Hungary its few sympathisers are scattered and closely watched, and its name is a byword for national catastrophe. Its leverage is confined to a small, ageing emigration and occasional contacts with the European neo-fascist scene.

22.name: Magyar Néphadsereg
22.text:
The Hungarian People's Army was rebuilt after 1956, when much of the old army had sided with the revolution or melted away. Some 100,000 strong, it is organised in motor rifle and tank divisions within the Warsaw Pact, alongside the Soviet Southern Group of Forces stationed on Hungarian soil. It is commanded by Defence Minister Lajos Czinege, in office since 1960, and Chief of the General Staff Károly Csémi.

Politically reliable and closely watched by party organs, the army took part in the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968. Its officers want modern Soviet equipment and a budget the reform economists would rather spend on consumption. Its leverage lies in its weapons and the trust of the Soviet command, but it has no tradition of acting alone.

23.name: Habsburg–Lotaringiai-ház
23.text:
The House of Habsburg-Lorraine wore the Hungarian crown from 1780 until 1918; King Charles IV twice tried to regain his throne in 1921 before dying in exile. His eldest son Otto von Habsburg, whom Hungarian legitimists regard as the rightful King Otto, lives in Pöcking in Bavaria, writes widely on European affairs and serves as vice-president of the Paneuropean Union.

Otto champions a united, Christian and anti-communist Europe in which the peoples of the old Danubian monarchy would be free again. Legitimism was strong among Catholic aristocrats and clergy before 1945, and Cardinal Mindszenty himself is a declared legitimist. At home the dynasty has no organised following, but its name stands for a Central European order older than both Trianon and Yalta.
